newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandan refugees flood across border into Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees flood across border into Rwanda.

text.p: Rwandan Hutu refugees at the head of a column estimated to number hundreds of thousands started pouring back into their homeland from Tanzania on Saturday.

The first passed through the Rusumo border crossing on bicycles, followed by an ever growing river of people on foot, belongings piled on their heads. Night fell and they were still streaming back to the homeland they had fled in 1994 after the Hutu-led genocide of Rwanda's minority Tutsis.
"We estimate thousands are crossing each hour," a World Food Programme (WFP) spokeswoman said.
She said the numbers crossing were so great that Rwandan authorities had asked aid agencies to move back health centres and food distribution points inside Rwanda so as not to impede the flow.
Tanzanian soldiers ordered all foreign journalists away from the Rusomo crossing. U.N. officials said the frontier would stay open beyond a normal closing time of 6 p.m. (1500 GMT).

Judith Melby, a spokeswoman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), estimated hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees were streaming towards Rusomo from as far away as Nyakahura, about 100 km (65 miles) to the southeast.

The exodus followed talks between camp leaders in Benaco and officials of the Tanzanian government, which announced last week that it wanted all 540,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tanzania to leave by December 31.

That announcement prompted hundreds of thousands of refugees to abandon their camps and move deeper into Tanzania to avoid repatriation. But many were stopped by Tanzanian soldiers at roadblocks and turned back.

It was the second mass return of Rwandan refugees since early November when more than 500,000 flooded out of Zaire within four days after a rebellion by Zairean Tutsis broke the stranglehold of extremist Hutu militia over the refugees in their camps.
Many Hutu refugees, two million of whom fled Rwanda in 1994, say they fear reprisals or punishment in revenge for the 1994 genocide of some 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
But human rights groups say the large numbers from eastern Zaire went home relatively safely. Rwanda's government says suspects will be prosecuted when investigations are complete.

Aid agencies have set up water points, health posts and biscuit distributions along a 100-km (65-mile) route in Rwanda. Some 200,000 of the refugees in Tanzania are from villages within 30 km (18 miles) of the Rusomo crossing and are expected to walk home.
It was unclear what would happen to Hutu hardline militiamen and former troops who refuse to go back because of their part in the genocide. There are also some 112,000 Burundian refugees in Tanzania.
WFP said more than 100,000 Rwandan refugees were still trekking southeast deeper into Tanzania.
"They have encountered some Tanzanian checkpoints and were urged to turn back but have not," said a WFP spokeswoman.
She said WFP staff had driven along the column, apparently made up of people fleeing Kitali and Keza camps and forests. UNHCR's Melby denied the report but WFP stuck to its account.
Aid workers fear large numbers of refugees will become scattered in the Tanzanian bush, just as happened to thousands of Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire last month.
Tanzanian authorities told UNHCR on Friday no Rwandan refugees would be allowed to remain in their camps.
UNHCR, which is barred by its mandate from cooperating with expulsions, says the repatriation is controlled by the military.
Soldiers beat refugees at Benaco camp with sticks on Friday as they rounded up those who fled away from Rwanda. They also used teargas and shot in the air to keep them on the road.
